issues.legal_issue: A decree-holder may pursue a personal remedy before resorting to charged property when the compromise decree gives an unqualified personal remedy and makes resort to the charge optional.
material_facts: The compromise decree required the judgment-debtors to pay a monthly allowance and provided that, after default, the decree-holder could recover the arrears by execution.
The decree separately charged specified property for payment and gave the decree-holder the option to recover from that property or to seek a receiver over it.
The decree-holder sought execution against other property while reserving her rights under the charge.
issues.conclusion: The personal remedy could be pursued without first exhausting the charged property or giving up the remedy under the charge.
issues.legal_principle: When a compromise decree provides both a personal remedy and a charge, whether the personal remedy may be pursued first depends on the intention gathered from the decree as a whole. Here the unqualified right to recover by execution, read with the separate language of liberty and option for remedies against the charged property, did not make resort to the charge a prerequisite. The court found it unnecessary to decide the cited Bombay decisions.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A decree-holder seeks to enforce a decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.compromise_decree_creates_personal_payme: The compromise decree makes one or more persons personally responsible for payment to the decree-holder.
predicates.personal_remedy_is_unqualified: The decree grants a right to recover personally without making that right dependent on first resorting to another remedy.
predicates.charge_remedy_is_optional: The decree describes recovery from charged property or through a receiver as an available option rather than a required first step.

issues.definition: When execution is sought under a compromise decree that imposes a personal payment duty, an unqualified personal remedy and an optional charge remedy permit personal recovery without first exhausting the charge.

issues.legal_issue: A beneficiary's interest in specifically allotted trust property is vested and attachable when the trust postpones enjoyment to facilitate payment of debts but its provisions otherwise show a present beneficial allocation, including succession to the beneficiary's heirs.
material_facts: A trust deed allotted specified lots of property to each of two beneficiaries after the trust ended upon payment of the settlor's debts and the settlor's death.
While the trust continued, specified monthly sums were paid to the settlor and the beneficiaries, and the remaining income was applied toward the debts.
The surplus income from each allotted lot was to pass with that lot to its designated beneficiary.

If a beneficiary died before the trust ended, the deed provided for the beneficiary's heirs to receive the relevant monthly payments and, in the case of the appellant, the property upon termination of the trust.
The appellant was a beneficiary and trustee, and the decree-holder sought attachment of property in the lots allotted to him.
One property was additionally subject to the other beneficiary's right of residence until alternative accommodation was provided.
issues.conclusion: The appellant had a vested beneficial interest in the allotted properties, and that interest was attachable; the additional residence right restricted enjoyment of the particular house but did not make the interest contingent.
issues.legal_principle: The character of an interest is determined by construing the whole instrument and discerning the settlor's intention, with a bias in favour of vesting unless a contrary intention is definite and clear. The court applied Transfer of Property Act, 1882, sections 19 and 21, and Indian Succession Act, 1925, sections 119 and 120, including the explanations to sections 19 and 119. It relied on the principle that postponement of enjoyment while income is applied for a beneficiary's benefit ordinarily indicates a vested interest. It also considered Ranganatha Mudaliar v. A. Mohana Krishna Mudaliar and Pestonjee Bhicajee v. P. H. Anderson, noting that a merely contingent interest is not attachable. The provisions for the beneficiary's heirs and the allocation of both the lots and their surplus income supported vesting. As to the house, the restriction on absolute enjoyment and the right of residence did not postpone vesting; the court construed them as limitations on enjoyment.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and trust_beneficial_interest_dispute and specified_property_lots_allocated_to_beneficiary and income_applied_to_debt_discharge_for_beneficiaries and (surplus_income_follows_allocated_lots and heirs_succeed_on_beneficiary_death) and enjoyment_restricted_by_residence_right

predicates.execution_proceeding: A decree-holder seeks attachment of property in proceedings to enforce a decree.
predicates.trust_beneficial_interest_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a judgment-debtor has an attachable beneficial interest under a trust.
predicates.specified_property_lots_allocated_to_ben: The trust instrument identifies particular property lots for a beneficiary to receive when the trust ends.
predicates.income_applied_to_debt_discharge_for_ben: The trust applies property income toward debts while providing some current payments for the beneficiaries or otherwise applying that income for their benefit.
predicates.surplus_income_follows_allocated_lots: The trust directs surplus income from an allocated lot to pass to the beneficiary designated to receive that lot.
predicates.heirs_succeed_on_beneficiary_death: The trust provides that the beneficiary's heirs receive the relevant benefit if the beneficiary dies before the trust ends.
predicates.enjoyment_restricted_by_residence_right: The trust limits a beneficiary's use or enjoyment of property by granting another person a right to reside there until an accommodation obligation is met.

issues.definition: When a trust allocates specified property to a beneficiary, applies income for the beneficiaries while discharging debts, directs surplus income to follow the allocated property, and provides for heirs to succeed, restrictions on enjoyment—including a residence right—do not prevent the beneficial interest from being vested and attachable.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise decree can be executed where its formal order incorporates the compromise, even if the order does not separately set out an express direction to pay.
material_facts: The compromise petition asked the court to record its terms and make them part of the decree.
The court ordered that the suit be decreed on compromise and that the compromise form part of the decree.
The decree did not separately set out an express direction requiring payment of the allowance.
issues.conclusion: Execution was not defeated by the absence of a separately stated payment direction in the formal decree.
issues.legal_principle: The court construed the formal order together with the incorporated compromise and concluded that the order conveyed the intended payment obligation for the purposes of execution. It noted that such a form was understood as having that effect in the usual practice described to the court, but expressed no opinion on whether that practice was correct. The objection arose in execution proceedings under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A decree-holder seeks to enforce a court order through execution proceedings.
predicates.compromise_terms_incorporated_into_forma: The formal court order makes the parties' compromise terms part of the decree.
predicates.formal_order_decrees_suit_on_compromise: The court formally disposes of the suit by decreeing it on the basis of the compromise.

issues.definition: When execution is sought and the formal order decrees the suit on compromise while incorporating the compromise terms, omission of a separate payment direction does not by itself defeat execution.
